blocks.content: COPY copies files or directories from the build context into the image's filesystem. It is the simplest, and most commonly used, way to get your application code into an image.
COPY takes a source path (relative to the build context) and a destination path inside the image, and copies the content across, becoming part of that layer's filesystem changes.

blocks.alt: Files move from the host context into the image

blocks.content: 2. The Source Must Be Inside the Build Context
blocks.text: 2. The Source Must Be Inside the Build Context

blocks.content: COPY cannot reach outside the build context at all, not a sibling directory, not an absolute host path. If a file is not inside the directory you pointed docker build at, COPY simply cannot see it.

blocks.alt: Nothing outside the build context is reachable

blocks.content: 3. Each COPY Creates Its Own Layer
blocks.text: 3. Each COPY Creates Its Own Layer

blocks.content: Like most Dockerfile instructions, COPY produces its own layer, which is exactly why the Image Caching topic recommends copying dependency manifests separately from application code, so a code-only change does not invalidate the (usually much slower) dependency install step.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: COPY moves files from the build context into the image, and can only reach files that are actually inside that context.
Splitting COPY calls (dependency files first, application code last) is a direct application of Docker's layer caching behavior.
